title: Targeted staff calls help mothers keep listening to mMitra health messages
summary: mMitra’s call scheduler reduced cumulative engagement drops by 32% compared with regular messaging alone over seven weeks.
account: ARMMAN tested a scheduler that selected mothers for live calls within its mMitra health-information program in India. The seven-week study began on 26 April 2021 and included 23,003 women. Participants received regular recorded messages, with two groups also receiving staff calls allocated either by the model or in rotation. Model-selected calls reduced cumulative engagement drops by 32.0% compared with messaging alone (p = .044) and by 28.3% compared with rotation-based calls (p = .098). The outcome counted weekly listening, not clinical health. Later studies examined revised models and health behaviors in other cohorts.
purpose: Allocate limited health-worker service calls to the beneficiaries whose program engagement they are most likely to preserve.
system: mMitra’s service-call scheduler, using a restless multi-armed bandit policy with clustered transition estimates and a random forest
developer: Google and Harvard University (Milind Tambe's group) with ARMMAN
taxonomy_note: The benefit concerns continued access to health information. It does not establish improved clinical health or retention of paying customers.

ratings.reason: The study found a measurable improvement in sustained access to health information, without establishing clinical health gains.
ARMMAN improved engagement within its limited capacity for staff calls.

ai_role.statement: The model selected participants for limited staff calls. The trial compared that policy with rotation-based calls and regular messaging alone. The developers and ARMMAN jointly conducted the study.
